item.content:encoded:
Current HDR Students

发布源: 9. Center for Water Economics, Environment and Policy, Crawford School, Australian NationalUniversity  – Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

CWEEP convenes public interest research on water economics and policy in Australia & the Asia-Pacific

The Centre for Water Economics, Environment and Policy (CWEEP – pronounced ‘sweep’) is a focal point for applied research, dialogues, policy and public engagement, and other work that contributes to improving the health and well-being of waterways and the human societies that dependent upon them.

Established in 2010 by Professor Quentin Grafton, CWEEP has convened policy-research dialogues, led applied research, and supported water education to strengthen water governance and environmental sustainability. Our research associates are leading researchers and practitioners whose expertise spans economics, institutional design, hydrology, geography, and beyond. Since 2024, CWEEP's work has been led by Dr Paul Wyrwoll with a focus on four core areas: dam reoperation, waterway restoration, the human right to water, and innovations in water pricing, markets and finance.

CWEEP’s research on water economics and policy is founded upon a systems perspective of trade-offs, decisions, and interactions. The scope of our work explicitly extends beyond understanding freshwater systems: we seek to inform and enable actions that address unsustainable water use, water injustice, and climate change. We value and support community-led research, deliberation, and advocacy that seeks to effect policy reform.

item.title: [Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia] Social Services Reforms
item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
Social Services Reforms

发布源: Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

In their current form, Australia’s social services are failing too many people.

Inaccessible, inconsistent, and unaffordable services are compounding inequality. Narrow eligibility criteria force people to navigate complex services or wait until they are in crisis.

From early childhood development to employment services, CPD works to change the way we deliver social services so that they truly work to support the community.

We envision a government that is more connected to communities, more hands-on, and that provides universally accessible, but not uniform, services that meet individuals’ needs.

Putting People Firstis a report that lays out a bold vision to transform social services to genuinely meet the needs of the people and communities they are designed to support.

It identifies six key drivers for reform and four practical steps governments can take now to create a system people can trust and depend on.

Growing Togetheris a report from the Centre for Policy Development’s early childhood development initiative, building on our landmarkStarting Betterreport andGuarantee for children and families.

It outlines essential steps for achieving a truly universal early education and care system.

Starting Betteris a landmark report from the Centre for Policy Development that proposes a guarantee for young children and families – a new pillar of Australia’s social deal.

Delivering the guarantee will make Australia the best place to be a child, and raise a family.

item.content:encoded:
Wellbeing Government in Australia

发布源: Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

Improving the wellbeing of current and future generations requires a shift in mindset when it comes to what we think ofas progress.

We promote policy approaches that meet the needs of people and the environment, that are values-driven, holistic and preventative.

Seeing policy ideas through a wellbeing lens leads to decisions that reflect community values, respect environmental bounds and deploy resources more effectively for the common good.

Our vision is to embed wellbeing at the heart of Australian policymaking in a way that will lead to effective and systemic change.

Avoidable Costsis a report that addresses the substantial costs governments incur by failing to address the root causes of issues, and makes the financial case for prevention and tackling problems early.

Embedding Progressis a report from the Centre for Policy Development that provides governments with a practical manual for how to achieve better outcomes for the people they serve.

TheWellbeing Economy in Briefseries is a collection of mini briefing papers that look at the idea of a wellbeing economy, how it relates to other ideas for economic change, and what some of the core elements of a wellbeing economy are.

item.content:encoded:
Specialist fees are hurting patients

发布源: Grattan Institute --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

by Peter Breadon, Mia Jessurun

Specialist doctors’ fees in Australia are out of control. Since 2023, specialist fees have grown three times faster than inflation.

It’s hurting patients and exacerbating the cost-of-living crisis. The federal government should step in to protect patients – including by withdrawing Medicare funding from the specialists who charge extreme fees.

The consequences of skyrocketing fees are serious. More than 800,000 Australians skip or delay specialist care due to cost each year – and that can mean missed diagnoses and worse outcomes.

As most of us know, seeing a specialist usually costs more than what Medicare will cover. Often, far more, leaving patients to pick up the bill.

The average patient fee for a specialist visit is $87. But for some specialties, fees are much higher. An initial visit to a dermatologist typically costs more than $200. For a psychiatrist, it typically costs a whopping $350.

This is not a new problem. Specialist fees have been rising for a long time.

Since 2010, they’ve increased every quarter, save for a brief reprieve during the height of COVID. Cumulatively, they increased by 183 per cent between 2010 and 2025 – three times faster than inflation, wages, or fees for other Medicare services.

New Grattan Institute analysis shows the trend has continued. In just the past year, specialist fees jumped another 4 per cent, on top of inflation.

item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Grattan Institute --Australia官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
Seeing a specialist keeps getting more expensive

发布源: Grattan Institute --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

by Peter Breadon, Thomas Shortridge

Seeing a specialist keeps getting more expensive, and a newGrattan Institute analysisshows the problem is getting worse, not better.

After years of inaction, reform may finally be on the agenda.

At the end of last year, Health Minister Mark Butler said fees to see medical specialists – such as paediatricians, dermatologists and psychiatrists – were “out of control”. The government has launched a parliamentary inquiry, and the federal health department has consulted on a range of reform options.

To make specialist medical care affordable, the consultations and inquiry must trigger overdue reform to train more specialists, fund more free public clinic appointments, and rein in the most extreme fees.

Our 2025 report,Special treatment, found that between 2010 and 2025, fees for specialist care outside hospitals grew 73% in real terms (meaning adjusted for inflation). That is many times faster than for GPs or other Medicare services. Since then, fee growth has continued unchecked. In the past year alone, specialist fees rose 4% faster than inflation.

Some specialties have seen especially steep rises. The median out-of-pocket fee for an initial psychiatry appointment is now A$351, up $90 in real terms in the past two years. The median initial dermatology appointment costs $217, up $28.

item.content:encoded:
Out of control: How to rein in runaway specialist fees

发布源: Grattan Institute --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

by Peter Breadon, Mia Jessurun, Thomas Shortridge

Specialist fees in Australia are out of control, and the government should protect patients by withdrawing Medicare funding from doctors who charge extreme fees.

Download the policy brief

Download the chart data

Since 2023, specialist doctors’ fees have grown three times faster than inflation.

In the past year, the median fee for an initial consultation with a dermatologist went up by 7 per cent, on top of inflation. For a psychiatrist, the increase was more than 20 per cent, with fees rising $50 a year in real terms.

Each year, more Australians pay far too much to see a specialist doctor.

Well over two million Australians now pay at least one extreme specialist fee a year – more than double the number in 2020.

This policy failure is hurting patients and exacerbating the cost-of-living crisis. Governments must train more specialists, expand public clinics, and step in to regulate extreme fees.

The policy brief comes a year after a Grattan report,Special treatment: Improving Australians’ access to specialist care, found some specialists charge more than three times the Medicare schedule fee.

This new policy brief shows that since then, fees have continued to go up.
